title: Zoox's Steering-Wheel-Free Robotaxis Get Green Light to Charge Passengers—a First in the U.S.
summary: Picture a car with no steering wheel, no pedals, and seats that face each other like a cozy campfire. Now imagine that car pulling up to the curb, ready to take you across town—and charge you for the trip. That's exactly what Zoox, an Amazon subsidiary, can now do. On Thursday, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) granted Zoox the first-ever exemption to operate a purpose-built, steering-wheel-free robotaxi for paid passengers. It's a watershed moment for the autonomous vehicle industry. While Waymo dominates the robotaxi market, its fleet still uses conventional vehicles with steering wheels and pedals—even its new, custom-built model retains those features to meet federal standards. Zoox, by contrast, has spent over a decade designing a vehicle from scratch that ditches traditional controls entirely. The NHTSA's two-year exemption allows Zoox to deploy up to 5,000 of its bidirectional, "campfire-style" vehicles. In exchange, the company must submit detailed reports on crashes and unexplained stops, and the agency can revoke the exemption if safety becomes a concern. NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison emphasized that Zoox demonstrated it exceeds the safety levels of conventional cars. "This technology needs to be developed appropriately, safely and responsibly," he said at an industry conference. "If we see an unreasonable risk to safety, you're going to hear from us." Morrison's caution is notable: earlier this month, he published an open letter citing a "clear pattern" of autonomous vehicles interfering with emergency responders, bluntly stating that an AV that can't safely interact with first responders is a public danger. Zoox has been offering free rides in Las Vegas since last year and is testing in Austin, Miami, and San Francisco. The company says it has autonomously transported over 500,000 riders across more than three million miles. Yet a recent voluntary recall—issued after discovering its cars might not properly detect smoke—revealed Zoox currently has just 105 active robotaxis. Scaling to 5,000 will be a monumental task. Meanwhile, Tesla is testing its own steering-wheel-free Cybercab but hasn't detailed how it will secure government approval. For now, its limited robotaxi service uses modified Model Ys with traditional controls. Zoox's approval is more than a regulatory win; it's a proof of concept that vehicles built for computers, not humans, can safely navigate our streets. As you read this, a driverless pod might be gliding through Las Vegas, ready to pick up its first paying customer. The future of transportation just got a little weirder—and a lot more exciting.
why_it_matters: Zoox’s approval shows that cars without human controls are no longer science fiction. In your lifetime, the way cities are built, how people commute, and what jobs exist could change completely because of machines that drive themselves—and the rules that try to keep everyone safe.

background_read: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA, the U.S. agency that sets vehicle safety standards) only rarely gives companies permission to skip standard rules. This is the first time it has exempted a fully driverless vehicle with no steering wheel or pedals.
Zoox was founded in 2014 and later bought by Amazon. It has spent years designing a car from scratch that treats the passenger cabin like a small room, with seats facing each other.

Waymo (a company owned by Alphabet, the parent of Google) started testing self-driving taxis in the 2010s, but always kept a steering wheel so a human could take over. Zoox’s approach is different—removing all controls changes what a car can look like and where it can drive.
The NHTSA recently warned that some autonomous vehicles failed to work safely around firefighters and police, raising concerns about public safety before giving Zoox this permission.

perspectives.description: Removing the steering wheel could make robotaxis roomier and more comfortable. Supporters believe purpose-built autonomous vehicles can eventually be safer than human drivers because they eliminate human error.

Critics worry that driverless cars that don’t work around emergency scenes put lives at risk. There is also concern about what happens to the millions of people who drive for a living if robotaxis become common.

This is not just a story about one company—it marks a shift in how regulators think about vehicles designed for AI instead of people. For decades, safety rules assumed a human could always take control; Zoox’s exemption rewrites that assumption.

If the idea works, future cities might look very different—fewer parking lots, new vehicle shapes, and public transport that blends with robotaxi fleets. But the path depends on whether the technology can earn public trust and safely coexist with emergency responders.
